title: Presenting Skills Without Overclaiming
summary: Bring the unit together by learning how to describe skills, evidence, projects, completion, and competency status accurately in resumes, interviews, portfolios, and career conversations.
objectives: Use language that matches the actual strength of available evidence.
Distinguish practiced, completed, demonstrated, reviewed, and verified claims.
Create a truthful skills-and-evidence presentation for a career conversation.

vocab.def: A statement that says something is true about your experience, skill, work, or status.
A statement that is appropriately backed by available evidence or institutional records.
A statement that goes beyond what the available evidence, verification, or authority actually supports.
Language that accurately explains the scope, status, limitation, or context of a claim.

sections.heading: Use language that matches the evidence
sections.body: There is an important difference between saying you practiced something, completed a related activity, demonstrated it in a project, submitted evidence, or received an authorized competency decision.

sections.heading: Completion claims should stay completion claims
sections.body: If you completed a course, say that you completed the course. Do not automatically convert completion into certification, mastery, licensure, or employment readiness.

sections.heading: Evidence can strengthen professional conversations
sections.body: Instead of relying only on labels, explain what you did and point to appropriate work samples or reviewed evidence when available.

sections.heading: Uncertainty can be communicated professionally
sections.body: When verification is pending or a claim has not been established, say so. Accurate status language builds more trust than pretending a decision has already been made.

practice.prompt: You completed an AI workplace literacy lesson and created a project, but no competency review occurred. Should you say 'verified AI professional'?
practice.answer: No. Describe the lesson and project accurately without inventing a verified qualification.

practice.prompt: A competency review is still pending. How should you describe it?
practice.answer: State that evidence was submitted or is awaiting review, rather than claiming the competency is already verified.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects responsible professional presentation?
options: Use claim language that matches the actual evidence, completion, and verification status
Turn every project into a verified competency
Treat course completion as professional licensure
quiz.answer: Use claim language that matches the actual evidence, completion, and verification status

lab.objective: Review a simulated learner record and create a truthful skills presentation separating activities, completed work, evidence candidates, reviewed evidence, competency decisions, and portfolio artifacts.

reflectionPrompt: How can using precise language about your skills make you more credible rather than less impressive?

proofActivity.title: Prove: present skills without overclaiming
proofActivity.description: Use relevant work samples or learning evidence to describe a skill accurately, distinguish supported evidence from unsupported claims, state limitations honestly, and identify an appropriate next step.
criteria: Connects a skill claim to relevant supporting evidence
Distinguishes demonstrated evidence from unsupported claims
Communicates an appropriate next step, request, or support need

prompts.observations: Evidence or work samples supporting the skill claim
prompts.uncertainty: What is not yet demonstrated, reviewed, or verified?
prompts.safeNextStep: Appropriate next step, request, or support need
